questions.prompt: Juftingizga ism kartasini ko‘rsating. Student, teacher, friend kartalaridan ikkitasini, kind va happy sifatlarini ayting. Tayyor “Hello!” qolipi bilan salomlashing; gap tuzish shart emas.
criteria: Ot va sifatni ajratish bo‘yicha berilgan vazifa bajarilgan.
Tayyor karta yoki o‘tilgan qolip to‘g‘ri tanlangan; hali o‘tilmagan zamon talab qilinmagan.
Sherik ko‘rsatilgan shaxs, buyum yoki ma’noni to‘g‘ri aniqlagan.

questions.prompt: To‘rtta yorliq yozing: ikki ot, ikki sifat. Keyin namunadan ikki sifat + ot birikmasini ko‘chiring.
expected:
student; teacher; kind; happy

a happy student
criteria: Topshiriqda so‘ralgan yorliq, gap yoki juftliklar to‘liq.
Ot va sifatni ajratish bo‘yicha kamida ikki to‘g‘ri misol bor.
Imlo va bosh harflar namunaga mos; mustaqil va ko‘chirilgan ish farqlangan.

questions.prompt: Otni yozing: happy / pencil / slowly.
questions.explanation: Pencil buyum nomi; shuning uchun ot. Happy sifat, slowly ravish.

questions.prompt: Shaxsni bildirgan otni yozing: run / teacher / kind.
questions.explanation: Teacher shaxs yoki kasb nomi. Run fe’l, kind bu ro‘yxatda sifat.

questions.prompt: Otni toping: quickly / hospital / tall.
questions.explanation: Hospital joy nomini bildirgan ot.

questions.prompt: Tanlang: There is a ___ outside. (bicycle / beautiful)
questions.explanation: A artiklidan keyin bu gapda buyum nomi kerak.

questions.prompt: Xato tasnifni tuzating: The table is large gapida table sifat deyilgan. To‘g‘ri turkumni tanlang: ot / fe’l.
questions.explanation: Table buyum nomi, shuning uchun ot.

questions.prompt: Swim fe’lidan shaxs oti yasang: a ___. (swimmer / swimming)
questions.explanation: Swimmer — suzuvchi shaxs nomi.

questions.prompt: Sifatni yozing: blue / bag / jump.
questions.explanation: Blue rangni bildiradi va otni tavsiflaydi.

questions.prompt: The tiny robot is here. Robotni tavsiflovchi sifatni yozing.
questions.explanation: Tiny robotning o‘lchamini bildiradi: juda kichik robot.

questions.prompt: The old bridge is safe. Yoshni bildiruvchi sifatni yozing.
questions.explanation: Old ko‘prikning eski ekanini bildiradi.

questions.prompt: Tanlang: It is a ___ road. (narrow / narrowly)
questions.explanation: Ot oldida uni tavsiflovchi sifat keladi.

questions.prompt: Faqat noto‘g‘ri so‘zni tuzating: The room is beautifully.
questions.explanation: Be dan keyin xonani tavsiflash uchun sifat kerak.

questions.prompt: Care otidan sifat yasang: a ___ driver. (careful / carefully)
questions.explanation: Careful haydovchining xususiyatini bildiradi.

Teacher: Ninety minutes.
Caller: How many students are in each group?
Teacher: Eight. Everyone has a work space.
Caller: How much clay do we use?
Teacher: About half a kilo each.
Caller: Who brings the tools?
Teacher: I bring them. You bring an apron.
Caller: How old is your youngest student?
Teacher: Seven. Her bowls are small, but her ideas are enormous.

sections.text: Yesterday was my grandfather's birthday. Our family was in the garden, but Grandfather wasn't there at first. He was in the kitchen with a large bowl of cherries. The garden was quiet because our surprise was a silent party. There were paper messages on every chair. My message was 'You are wonderful!' My little brother's message was only a picture of a cake. He is six, and long words are difficult for him. Grandfather was very happy with the messages. His eyes were wet, but he wasn't sad. The cake was small and slightly crooked. My brother was proud of it. At the end, everyone was noisy again. A silent party is lovely, but a family of twelve isn't silent for long.

sections.transcript:
Guide: Hello, Nargiza. Was your school trip good yesterday?
Nargiza: Yes, it was. The dinosaur room was wonderful.
Guide: Were all your classmates there?
Nargiza: No, they weren't. Aziz was at home with a cold. There were nineteen of us.
Guide: Was the weather nice?
Nargiza: No. Our shoes were wet, but the museum was warm. My socks were two different colours, so everyone was cheerful.
Guide: Was your teacher angry about the noise?
Nargiza: No, she wasn't. She was interested in a tiny dinosaur egg.
Guide: And the cafe?
Nargiza: The cafe wasn't open. Our sandwiches were in our bags, so that wasn't a problem. My sandwich was enormous. The dinosaur was big, but my lunch was impressive too.
Guide: A very memorable trip! Nargiza: Our teacher was happy with our questions too.

sections.text: Yesterday our technology club tested a painting robot. We attached a brush to a small toy car and placed paper on the floor. The car moved slowly and painted a blue line. It stopped near my shoe, but it didn't touch it. We wanted a picture of a river. Unfortunately, the second line looked like a very tired snake. Our teacher didn't laugh at the picture. sections.text: Two days ago our street held an umbrella race. It wasn't a running race. Each team decorated an umbrella and walked slowly across the square. My sister and I made a yellow sun on ours. We started at eleven, just before a light shower. Other teams carried fish, flowers and even a tiny paper castle above their heads. Who won the prize? A quiet man with a plain black umbrella won it. sections.title: Week 9 · The Missing Seed Tray
sections.text: Yesterday our school gardening club opened its spring fair. There were six trays on the table at nine, but at ten there were only five. We looked under the table and checked the empty boxes. Nothing was there. Then our teacher asked the caretaker. He moved one tray to the sunny window before the visitors arrived. Its label was wet, so he put a new label beside it. We carried the tray back and wrote its price clearly. Nobody stole any plants. We sold all six trays before lunch and kept the empty pots for next month.

sections.text: At half past six yesterday morning, our bakery was already busy. My aunt was mixing dough in a large bowl. Her assistant was arranging round loaves on a tray, and I was writing prices on a board. I wasn't baking anything; I am still learning. Outside, a man was waiting with an empty basket. He wasn't looking at the bread. He was looking at our window display, because a toy bear was sitting between two enormous loaves. The bear was wearing a paper hat. We were preparing a display for Children's Day, and the bear was our new baker. In the corner, the radio was playing quiet music. Our real cat was sleeping under a chair. It wasn't helping, but nobody expected much work from the cat before breakfast.

sections.text: My grandmother keeps an old shopping basket beside her modern bicycle. She used to walk to the market every morning. She didn't use to carry a phone or a shopping list. She remembered everything, except salt. There was always one forgotten packet of salt. The market used to have only six stalls, and the fruit seller used to know every customer's name. Presenter: Welcome back to our town radio. What was this studio like twenty years ago, Karim?
Karim: We used to record everything on tape. We didn't use to have computers on these desks.
Presenter: How did you find music?
Karim: We used to keep records in a tall cupboard. The labels were handwritten, and my writing was terrible.
Presenter: That sounds difficult.
Karim: It was. One morning I played a duck sound instead of the weather music. Our listeners were very amused.
Presenter: Did you work alone?
Karim: No. Three people used to prepare the morning show. We didn't use to record at home. Everyone came here, even during heavy snow.
Presenter: And this red chair?
Karim: It used to belong to our news reader. It made a loud squeak. Sometimes the chair was louder than the news.

sections.text: Our town hall used to have a very unreliable clock. Every Monday, the caretaker would climb the stairs and check its mechanism. People used to joke about the town's extra ten minutes. Last autumn, our history club visited the tower. We were examining the heavy door when a strange noise came from above. It sounded like a giant sneeze. Was the caretaker working inside? No, he wasn't. He was waiting for us downstairs. While we were looking up, a pigeon flew out of a narrow window. A loose metal panel moved behind it and made the noise again. The caretaker fixed the panel that afternoon. The clock still showed the wrong time, but the tower stopped sneezing. Our guide wrote down the incident in the visitors' book, beside our ordinary names.

Student: Did you use to teach in this room, Ms Eva?
Teacher: Yes. It used to be a furniture shop before our dance school opened.
Student: What were lessons like then?
Teacher: We would move the remaining chairs against the wall. Then we would practise in the centre. The floor was wonderful, but the mirror was tiny.
Student: Did anything funny happen?
Teacher: Once, I was demonstrating a slow turn when a customer entered with a broken chair.
Student: Was he looking for the furniture shop?
Teacher: Yes, he was. While I was explaining the change, my students were balancing on one foot behind me.
Student: What did the customer do?
Teacher: He laughed and stayed for a trial lesson. He didn't repair his chair that day, but he learned three dance steps. He still comes every Thursday.

sections.title: Week 10 · The Lantern on the River
sections.text: When my mother was a child, families used to meet beside the river for a lantern evening. They would bring food and hang paper lanterns in the trees. Last autumn we returned to the same place. While we were unpacking supper, a strong wind blew one lantern into the water. My brother reached for a stick, but a boat owner was already moving towards it. She lifted it out and brought it to us. The paper was ruined, but the small battery light still worked. We put the light in a glass jar. My mother said the old tradition had found a new container.

sections.text: Our school is starting an umbrella library on Monday. Students are going to borrow umbrellas at reception and return them the next day. The first collection contains twelve umbrellas in bright colours. The service opens at eight, before lessons begin. I am meeting the receptionist at seven forty to arrange the stand. sections.text: The youth centre's project room looks different today. Our team has painted the walls pale blue and moved the heavy cupboards away from the windows. I have made a reading corner with three cushions. Aziz has built a low table from an old wooden door, and two volunteers have brought colourful lamps. The room has become bright and welcoming. On the noticeboard, we have written a list of completed jobs. The list includes 'Find the mysterious smell'. Our leader has found its source: a forgotten cheese sandwich inside a cardboard box. She has removed the box, and everyone has opened a window. Now the room smells of fresh paint instead. We have taken a group photograph beside the new table. The old door has a new job, and so do we.

Volunteer: Have you finished the shelter newsletter, Sara?
Sara: Almost. I have already written the story about Momo, the rabbit. He went to his new home yesterday.
Volunteer: Have you included the dog walk?
Sara: Yes. We have organised four walks this month. Last Saturday's walk raised enough money for twelve blankets.
Volunteer: Has the photographer sent the pictures yet?
Sara: No, she hasn't. She has gone to another event, but she promised to send them tonight.
Volunteer: How long has she helped us?
Sara: Since March. She has never missed a newsletter deadline.
Volunteer: Good. What has happened to the old office chair?
Sara: We have moved it into the quiet room. Our oldest cat has already claimed it.
Volunteer: Then please add a photograph of our new manager. He works for biscuits and sleeps through meetings.

sections.text: Our neighbourhood game cupboard has been open for three months. Volunteers have checked every donated game, and they have replaced missing pieces in eight boxes. Last Friday a family brought a large puzzle. We counted its pieces yesterday and found one missing corner. We haven't put it on the borrowing shelf yet. Mina has already contacted the family, but they haven't replied. I have used the cupboard twice this week. I borrowed a word game on Monday and returned it on Wednesday. The cupboard has made our evenings more sociable. However, we still record each loan carefully; being friendly doesn't mean forgetting who has each box.

sections.text: For the past three weeks, our craft club has been knitting a giant scarf for the statue outside the library. The librarian has been helping us choose colours, and local families have been donating spare wool. We haven't been working every day; we meet on Tuesday and Thursday evenings. The scarf is nearly four metres long now. Have we been measuring it carefully? Yes, because the statue has unusually broad shoulders. My brother has been counting the stripes and recording their colours in a notebook. He hasn't been knitting, but his record prevents arguments about the pattern. Yesterday a visitor asked about the enormous scarf. We explained our winter display project. The statue is made of stone and doesn't feel cold, but the bright scarf is giving the grey square a warmer appearance.

Why hadn't anyone carried it into the hall? The receptionist had left a note for the afternoon volunteer, but he hadn't seen it. He had put a large flower arrangement on top of the paper. We searched the building for ten minutes before the cook opened the cupboard. The cake was perfect, and the candles were beside it. The host thanked everyone and placed the flowers somewhere else. Our anniversary celebration finally began with excellent cake and a lesson about visible messages.

sections.text: When I visited my neighbour's workshop yesterday, her hands were blue and the floor was covered with newspaper. She had been painting a wooden cupboard for three hours. She hadn't been using gloves because she couldn't find a pair small enough for her hands. Had she finished the whole cupboard? No, she hadn't. She had painted the doors, but the sides were still brown. Before I arrived, she had moved the shelves into the garden. Then the wind became stronger, so we carried them inside together. Her dog watched from the doorway and kept a careful distance from the paint. We put a clean sheet under the shelves and made tea. By then, my hands were blue too. The cupboard had gained colour, and I had gained an unexpected afternoon project.

sections.text: Our astronomy club has been restoring an old telescope for a month. We have cleaned the lenses and replaced a damaged screw. Last Friday, however, the first test failed. We had been adjusting the stand for nearly an hour when the teacher noticed a loose joint. We hadn't tightened it properly, so the image shook whenever someone touched the table. After we fixed the joint, the telescope worked. We had expected a serious problem, but the solution was small. Since that evening, we have observed the moon twice. I have been keeping a record of our observations in a notebook. The first page contains a drawing of the moon; the second contains a large reminder about screws. Scientific discoveries are exciting, but sometimes they begin with ordinary checking and a very small tool.

sections.title: Week 13 · The Roof Garden Record
sections.text: Our class has been measuring the roof garden temperature for a month. We have collected twenty readings, but two are unusable. On Tuesday, the thermometer showed an unusually high number. Before taking that reading, someone had left it beside a warm ventilation pipe. We had been using the same shaded corner for three weeks, so the change of position mattered. We marked Tuesday's result as unreliable instead of deleting it without explanation. Today we have moved the thermometer back. Our report isn't finished yet. We have been checking the notes against photographs, and we will explain why two readings cannot support our conclusion. A long table is less useful than a trustworthy one.

sections.text: Our walking club tested two routes to the river on Sunday. The hill route is shorter than the canal route, but it is steeper and more tiring. It took us thirty minutes. The canal route took forty minutes, although the path is flatter and easier for beginners. My uncle prefers the hill because the view is better from the top. My aunt prefers the canal because the benches are more comfortable and the traffic noise is lower. We carried the same small backpack on both walks, so our comparison was fair. Near the canal, a duck followed us for several metres. It seemed more interested in our sandwiches than in our research. Next week we are taking new members along the canal. A longer walk with comfortable breaks is more suitable for that group.

Buyer: I'm choosing between these two chairs for my sewing room.
Seller: The wooden chair is cheaper, but the padded one is more comfortable during long sessions.
Buyer: My room is small. Which chair is narrower?
Seller: The wooden one. It fits under this desk easily. The padded chair is wider because of its arms.
Buyer: Is the wooden chair lighter too?
Seller: Yes, by two kilograms. It's easier to move when you clean the floor.
Buyer: The padded seat feels better, though. I work for several hours at a time.
Seller: You could add a cushion to the wooden chair.
Buyer: That's a useful compromise. My cat already thinks every cushion belongs to her.
Seller: Then a removable cushion is safer. You can keep it in the cupboard between sewing sessions and avoid a daily argument about ownership.

sections.text: Our school shop compared two ways of packing books for delivery. The first group used loose paper and ordinary tape. The second group used folded cardboard corners. Both groups had some small boxes, but there weren't any large ones. The second group worked more slowly at first because the folds needed care. After ten minutes, they packed books much faster than before. Their parcels also survived our gentle shaking test more successfully. The first group finished a bit earlier, but some books moved inside the boxes. We didn't find any damaged covers, although the movement was worrying. Our shop leader suggested another practice round before choosing a method. Fast packing is useful, but books need to arrive safely. The cardboard corners looked rather like tiny hats, so we called the trial 'Fashion Week for Novels'.

sections.text: Our hiking group inspected two tents before a weekend trip. Both of them were clean, but neither was perfect. The green tent had enough space for three people, although it was too heavy for our youngest members to carry. The orange tent was light, but there was little room for bags inside. We had a little money left in the equipment budget, enough for one waterproof storage cover. Most of the group preferred the orange tent with bags outside under that cover. Two members preferred the green one because they wanted everything indoors. All of us agreed that either tent was safe in mild weather. None of the poles were damaged. Finally, we chose the orange tent and the cover. Our leader reminded us that dry socks matter more than a bedroom large enough for a dance party.

sections.text: Our student council compared three donated school bags before choosing a model for next year's collection. The red bag was the cheapest and lightest, but its straps were too thin for heavy books. The grey bag had more pockets and stronger stitching. The black bag was as strong as the grey one, although it cost much more. We put the same books and a full water bottle in each bag. Most of the testers chose the grey model because it carried the weight more comfortably. A few preferred the red one for short trips. None of the bags was waterproof, so we suggested buying some simple rain covers too. There was enough money for twenty grey bags and twenty covers. Our final recommendation included that exact quantity rather than a vague request for 'lots of bags'.

Coordinator: We expect forty guests. Is there enough tea?
Helper: Yes, but there are only thirty cups. We need a few more.
Coordinator: The reusable cups are more expensive to rent than paper ones, but they are stronger.
Helper: They're also easier to carry when full. Both suppliers can deliver before noon.
Coordinator: Which supplier is cheaper?
Helper: The local cafe, by ten thousand som. It doesn't have many large plates, though.
Coordinator: We don't need large plates. Most of the food is small sandwiches.
Helper: Shall I order forty-five cups and some small plates?
Coordinator: Yes. A little extra capacity is useful, but we don't need twice as much as the guest count.
Helper: Agreed. Last time we had enough cups for an imaginary second wedding.
Coordinator: This time let's keep the order realistic and the cupboard clear.

sections.title: Week 14 · Choosing a Delivery Basket
sections.text: Our library tested two bicycle baskets. The metal basket was cheaper and stronger than the woven one, but it was also heavier. Both held ten small books. Neither kept rain out, so each needed a cover. The woven basket was easier to lift, and our older volunteer preferred it. We had enough money for two metal baskets with covers or one woven basket with a cover. Two volunteers usually deliver at the same time. The team chose the metal baskets for the shared bikes and kept a lightweight bag for the older volunteer. The cheapest choice was not automatically the best; the decision depended on how many people needed equipment and what they could comfortably carry.

sections.text: When my aunt was ten, she could cycle across the village without stopping, but she couldn't swim. Her school was near a river, and she watched other children from the bank. Could her parents teach her? No, they couldn't; neither of them was a confident swimmer. A new sports teacher later started lessons at a shallow outdoor pool. At first, my aunt could only put her face in the water for a second. After several weeks, she could float and move across the small pool. She still couldn't dive, but that wasn't the teacher's first goal. Today she takes her grandchildren swimming and understands their nervousness. She keeps her old swimming cap in a drawer. It is bright orange and rather ugly, but it reminds her that ability often grows through many small attempts.

sections.transcript:
Interviewer: Could you draw well as a child, Mr Saidov?
Painter: I could copy simple pictures, but I couldn't draw faces. Every person looked slightly surprised.
Interviewer: Could you paint large letters then?
Painter: Not at first. My father painted shop signs, and I watched him after school. By thirteen, I could paint neat capital letters with a wide brush.
Interviewer: What was difficult?
Painter: I couldn't keep the spacing even. Some words looked as if the letters were arguing and moving apart.
Interviewer: Could your father explain the spacing?
Painter: Yes, he could. He used pencil marks and showed me how to measure each gap.
Interviewer: Do you still use that method?
Painter: Often. Computers help with design now, but measuring carefully is still useful when the real wall isn't perfectly straight.

One evening, my roommate wanted hot tea while she worked on her presentation. She wrote a polite note to reception: 'I would like some hot water for tea. We also moved our evening study session earlier, so future tea breaks no longer required a small diplomatic mission.

sections.text: Our community centre held a recording day for older residents. Some visitors could tell long stories easily but couldn't use the recording software. Student volunteers could manage the equipment, although they needed help with unfamiliar place names. We paired people according to these different abilities. Visitors were allowed to choose whether their recordings stayed private or joined the public collection. One participant asked, 'Could you stop the recording for a moment?' She wanted to check a date with her sister. We paused immediately. Later, we managed to repair a loose microphone connection without losing any files. By the afternoon, we had recorded eight interviews. Next month, the volunteers will be able to edit them after additional training. The project showed that technical confidence and personal knowledge are different strengths, and both deserve respect.

sections.title: Week 15 · Recording the Village Song
sections.text: Our music club can record interviews, but we can't remove every background sound. Last week a gardener sang an old village song for us. We were able to finish the recording before the lawnmower started, although we couldn't stop a nearby bird. The gardener said we could share the song at school, but he didn't give permission to put it online. 'Could you send me a copy first?' he asked. We agreed. One student suggested asking him to record again indoors. Another said the bird made the recording feel natural. The club will ask the gardener what he prefers. Technical ability and permission are separate questions: a clear recording isn't automatically ours to publish everywhere.

sections.text: Before our first practical session, the workshop leader explained three essential rules. We must wear safety glasses when cutting wire. We must keep bags away from the central walkway, and we mustn't touch plugged-in equipment during repairs. One student asked, 'Must we wear gloves for every task?' The leader explained that different tools need different protection, so we must follow each demonstration carefully. He showed us a damaged cable and disconnected it before touching the wires. The rules were specific, not simply a long list of frightening words. At the end, we practised arranging a safe work area without switching on any tools. My partner placed his sandwich beside the repair parts. The leader smiled and moved it to the break table. Even a hungry technician must distinguish lunch from spare components.

Leader: Before we begin the nature walk, everyone must stay with a partner. We mustn't leave the marked path.

sections.text: New members of our community garden receive a short welcome guide. It separates rules from advice. Members mustn't leave tools across the paths, because other gardeners may trip over them. They don't have to buy their own tools; shared equipment is available in the shed. The guide recommends arriving early during hot weather. Gardeners should bring drinking water and a hat, but they shouldn't work for long without a break. Nobody has to finish a whole bed in one visit. Our coordinator checks that beginners choose manageable tasks. Last summer, one enthusiastic volunteer tried to weed three beds before lunch and became exhausted. Now he helps explain the guide. He calls himself the garden's example of excessive ambition. His advice is friendly: a small area done carefully is better than a large area abandoned halfway through.

sections.text: After our college open day, the volunteer team reviewed the instructions. Visitors had to sign in at reception, but they didn't have to book ordinary campus tours. They mustn't enter laboratories without a guide, and that rule was clearly displayed. Some information was less clear. Volunteers had printed extra maps, although reception already had enough. They needn't have used that paper. Next time, we will have to check supplies before ordering more. We should also place signs at the side entrance because several families missed the main desk. The aim is a welcoming visit with understandable rules, not a day spent guessing what each coloured arrow means.

sections.title: Week 16 · Rules for the Borrowed Projector
sections.text: The community centre lends its projector to local clubs. Borrowers must sign the register and mustn't leave the machine in a parked car. They don't have to bring their own cable; one is included. At the previous meeting, we had to borrow an extra extension lead because the socket was far from the screen. This time the organiser has checked the room in advance. She says we should test the picture before the audience arrives. We needn't print fifty handouts because only twenty people have booked. Anyone using photographs ought to check permission from the people shown. The rules protect the equipment, while the advice helps the event run well. Confusing advice with a ban can make a simple service unnecessarily difficult.

sections.text: The noticeboard outside our community centre has been empty since Monday. Usually, it advertises language clubs, repairs and lost cats with surprisingly professional photographs. Several residents think the centre is closing, but the manager has not announced any closure. There are other possible explanations. The printer may be broken, or the volunteer may be away. The online calendar still shows three events for next week, although that information could be old. A cleaner saw a box of new drawing pins in the office yesterday. That detail suggests somebody plans to use the board again, but it does not prove when. I asked two neighbours before writing a message to the manager. One wanted to warn everyone immediately; the other preferred to wait. I chose a question rather than a warning. An empty board might mean a communication problem. It may not mean an empty building.

sections.text: Three framed photographs arrived at our youth centre without a sender's note. They showed the old railway bridge, so they might belong to the local history group. However, the group's organiser denied sending them. A delivery label carried yesterday's date, which meant the parcel couldn't have been waiting in our office for weeks. We should have recorded the driver's details, but reception had been busy. The frames were new, and someone must have spent money preparing the pictures. That made throwing them into storage a poor response. We posted a neutral description online without publishing the photographs. By evening, a former member contacted us. She had intended them for next month's exhibition but had forgotten the note. We could have guessed correctly, yet a careful enquiry worked better. Clear labels are likely to become a firm rule for future donations, alongside a rather less official request for readable handwriting.

Analyst: The phone bookings are normal. That supports your idea. We should have tested the update before releasing it.
Manager: Could customers be giving up at the payment screen?

sections.title: Week 17 · The Closed Workshop
sections.text: The pottery workshop was locked when three students arrived at two. A light was on upstairs, but nobody answered the bell. 'The teacher must have forgotten us,' one student said. Another noticed a note inside the glass door, too far away to read. The third checked their booking message: it said half past two, not two. The teacher might have been preparing upstairs, or the light could have been left on by someone else. Neither possibility was confirmed. The students waited in the café opposite and sent a message. At two twenty-five, the teacher opened the door and apologised for missing the bell. She had been moving clay in the back room. The unreadable note gave the afternoon opening time. The incident showed that a plausible explanation can still be wrong, especially when a small detail in the original evidence has been overlooked.

sections.text: Our gardening group keeps a notebook of repeated problems. If seedlings get too little light, they grow long and weak. If we water them too heavily, the soil stays wet and the roots struggle. These statements describe regular patterns, not one future experiment. Last month, we moved half the trays to a brighter window and kept the other half on the original shelf. The brighter group grew shorter, stronger stems. However, light was not the only difference: the window area was also cooler. We therefore avoid claiming that our small comparison proves everything. What happens if we change two conditions at once? We cannot easily identify the cause of an improvement. Our next trial will change only the location of the lamp. The notebook has become more valuable than our enthusiastic guesses. Even the tray labelled 'Guaranteed Success' now carries a question mark, which is probably its most scientific feature.

sections.transcript:
Trainer: What happens if two people edit the same event without checking each other?
Assistant: We sometimes get conflicting times. If the organiser doesn't name an owner, everyone assumes somebody else will check it.
Trainer: Exactly. If an event has one named owner, questions reach the right person. That doesn't mean nobody else can help.
Assistant: Our volunteers worry that ownership means extra work.
Trainer: It usually means a clear point of contact. If the owner is away, a deputy takes over. We write both names on the calendar.
Assistant: And if the time changes?
Trainer: The owner updates the calendar and sends a message. If people only change the calendar, some participants miss the news.
Assistant: So the system needs a record and a notification.
Trainer: Yes. A perfect calendar is not useful if nobody knows it has changed. Our old one was accurate in the same way a secret is accurate: quietly, and for very few people.

sections.text: Our street association wants a tool library. If people share rarely used equipment, they save storage space and avoid buying the same things repeatedly. That general benefit sounds convincing, but borrowing needs rules. If the pilot opens next month, members will book tools through a simple paper register. Unless a volunteer checks an item on return, damage may go unnoticed. One resident imagines a digital system with automatic lockers. If we had a larger budget, that would be attractive, but we currently have enough money only for shelves and basic repairs. The proposal therefore begins with twenty donated tools and two opening evenings a week. Would more residents join if collection were available on Saturday? The committee will ask before fixing the schedule. A useful service must match people's lives. There is little point in sharing a drill if its opening hours require everyone to become an expert in rearranging their working week.

sections.transcript:
Facilitator: If people bring dishes without labels, guests with allergies cannot choose safely. That is our first rule: label ingredients.
Member: If everyone agrees, we'll hold the lunch next Thursday. What will we do if it rains?
Facilitator: We'll use the downstairs room. Unless the lift is working, we won't use the upper floor.
Member: Good. If we had a professional kitchen, we could cook together, but our room only has a kettle.
Facilitator: Then food should arrive ready to eat. If I were you, I would choose something simple to transport.
Member: Would you include neighbours outside the association?
Facilitator: Yes, if we had enough places. For this pilot, we'll reserve ten seats for them and review attendance afterwards.
Member: That balances welcome and capacity.
Facilitator: Exactly. A community lunch needs generosity, but it also needs enough chairs and accurate information about the mysterious green sauce.

sections.title: Week 18 · A Cooler Waiting Area
sections.text: Our clinic is considering a shaded waiting area outside. If metal seats stand in direct sun, they become uncomfortable. If the council approves the plan, volunteers will install a canopy next month. The receptionist supports the idea because the indoor room is crowded on market days. A nurse is less certain: if patients wait outside, staff may not hear them ask for help. She suggests a bell and clear signs. One resident says that if she had more money, she would donate a water dispenser too. That is an imagined contribution, not a confirmed offer. The clinic will try the canopy for four weeks before making it permanent. If the trial reveals new difficulties, the team will adjust the arrangement. The aim is to increase comfort without making it harder for vulnerable patients to contact staff.

sections.text: Our free repair event had tools, volunteers and a cheerful poster. Unfortunately, the poster gave the date but not the address. We shared it online on Wednesday and waited for a busy Saturday. Only regular visitors came. If we had included the address, new residents would have found us more easily. If one person had checked the poster as an outsider, the omission would probably have been obvious. We had all worked in the centre for years, so its location felt like common knowledge. The mistake was not a lack of enthusiasm; it was an assumption about our audience. After the event, we asked two newcomers to review our next announcement. They also wanted bus information and a contact number. If we hadn't made the first mistake, we might not have noticed these wider needs. That does not make the mistake desirable, but it gives the disappointing afternoon a useful consequence.

sections.text: A local historian agreed to speak at our youth club, but her train was cancelled. We nearly abandoned the session. Instead, one volunteer suggested a phone interview through a speaker. Would we have tried that if our audience had already arrived? Probably not; the extra hour gave us time to test the sound. What might have happened if we had cancelled immediately? Some visitors might have lost interest in future events, although we cannot know that for certain. The remote format had disadvantages: questions were slower, and the historian could not show her maps clearly. However, we recorded the audio with her permission and later added photographs of the maps. If we had insisted on a perfect live event, we could have missed a useful alternative. The result was not identical to our original plan. It was a different event with different strengths, including a historian speaking from her kitchen beside an occasionally opinionated kettle.

sections.text: Our class is planning a garden visit with several older neighbours. One resident said, 'I wish I could walk the whole route, but my knee makes that difficult.' The organiser replied that shorter routes were available. We hope the weather stays dry, but we will bring portable seats even if the forecast is good. Comfort should not depend on luck. The garden manager allows us to use the sheltered terrace provided we leave it clean. Volunteers can borrow wheelchairs as long as they return them before closing time. These conditions are practical, not signs of reluctance to welcome us. A student first suggested cancelling the longer walk for everyone. However, residents preferred a choice of routes and a shared tea break afterwards. Inclusion does not always mean doing exactly the same activity. It can mean giving people enough information and support to choose. Our plan now has more options and fewer assumptions about what others need.

If we had checked access with a wheelchair user beforehand, we would have noticed the problem. I wish we had asked people about their needs instead of assuming that a short distance was automatically easy. If our information sheet were clearer, visitors would have known about the steps before registering. The guide changed the route and brought the group back together at the market, but some trust was lost. We now hope the next walk will rebuild it. A volunteer offered to test alternative routes as long as the team shared the full plan early. We accepted. The aim is not to advertise a perfect service after one correction. It is to show that feedback changes decisions. A route is not accessible merely because an enthusiastic organiser can walk it quickly.

Chair: I wish we had placed the labels lower. Several visitors couldn't read them comfortably.
Designer: If I had seen the room with the chairs in place, I would have noticed the height problem.
Visitor: And if the lighting were brighter, I would have stayed longer yesterday. The pictures were interesting, but reading was tiring.
Chair: Would larger print have helped as well?

Designer: We can test a new label provided you are willing to comment on it.

Chair: Good. Our success should depend on visitors understanding the stories, not on the labels looking elegant from across an empty room.

sections.text: At our community cafe, reusable cups are collected at a separate counter. Staff check each cup, and damaged ones are removed from service. The remaining cups are washed, dried and stored upside down. This process sounds simple, but customers often leave cups in the paper recycling bin. A sign saying 'Staff collect cups here' was replaced with 'Cups are collected here', beside a large arrow. The new wording puts the object in focus, which helps people looking for somewhere to return it. However, grammar alone cannot fix poor placement. The first sign stood behind a plant, where it was almost invisible. We moved it to eye level and watched what happened over three busy afternoons. Incorrect returns fell noticeably. We cannot separate the effect of wording from the effect of position, but together the changes helped. The plant still has a place in the cafe; it no longer manages customer information.

Mechanic: Every bicycle is labelled with a number. Its brakes and tyres are checked before anybody rides it.

sections.text: The community centre's new booking system has been tested by twelve volunteers. Several confusing buttons have been renamed, and a large-print guide has been prepared. However, the payment feature has not been approved yet, so the system is not ready for public use. Has the old booking method been removed? No. Telephone bookings are still available, and staff are keeping a paper record during the transition. The project leader wants to announce success, but the volunteers argue that progress and completion are different things. One important task remains unfinished even though many smaller tasks have been completed. Their report lists what has changed, what still needs checking and who will make the final decision. This is less exciting than a banner saying 'Finished!', but more useful to users. A system should not graduate from testing simply because everyone is tired of talking about it. Readiness needs evidence, not an enthusiastic exclamation mark.

Journalist: Has the photo collection been digitised completely?
Archivist: Most of it has been scanned, but forty fragile photographs haven't been processed yet.
Journalist: Have the owners' names been checked?
Archivist: Yes. The names have been compared with the donation records. Some dates are still uncertain, and they have been labelled as estimates.
Journalist: Why not leave those dates out?
Archivist: An approximate date can help, provided readers know its limits. We don't want a guess to look like a verified fact.

Journalist: So the work is close, but not complete.
Archivist: Exactly. Preserving history includes preserving uncertainty. Otherwise, a neat caption can accidentally create a story that never happened, which would make our archive very organised and rather unreliable.

sections.text: The drinking fountain in our park was installed twenty years ago, but it stopped working last spring. A damaged valve was found during an inspection. The fountain is now being repaired, and the surrounding path is being levelled for easier access. New water tests have been completed, although the final result has not been published yet. Until then, the fountain is not used by the public. Some residents think the delay proves the project is badly managed. Others point out that safe operation requires more than a shiny tap. The council's update gives dates for completed work and explains the remaining test. It could still be clearer about the expected reopening. Our residents' group has requested a weekly update rather than a promise without evidence. The fountain is a small facility, but the discussion reveals a larger issue: trust grows when people can distinguish work in progress from work that is genuinely ready.

sections.title: Week 20 · Where the Repair Record Goes
sections.text: Every donated kettle at the reuse centre is checked before it is offered to a new owner. A volunteer records the model number, but electrical testing is carried out by a trained technician. Last month several labels were damaged during cleaning. The kettles had been tested, yet the results could not be matched confidently to individual machines. They were removed from the display until new checks were completed. Now a duplicate record is kept in the office. Customers are told what was tested and when, rather than simply being assured that an item is 'fine'. The centre has not found evidence that the affected kettles were dangerous. The problem was the missing link between each object and its test result. Reliable records make an assurance checkable; they do not turn used equipment into something guaranteed never to fail.

sections.text: The town square will be closed to private cars for one trial weekend next month. Temporary benches will be placed near the trees, and a marked delivery route will be kept open before ten each morning. The permanent parking layout will not be changed during the trial. That distinction matters because some residents have read the announcement as a final decision. Visitor numbers, shop sales and access problems will be recorded, but no single measure will determine the outcome. A busy square may benefit cafes while creating difficulties for other businesses. The report will therefore include comments from traders, disabled visitors and delivery drivers. Supporters want the experiment to succeed, yet a useful trial must be allowed to reveal problems. If every difficulty is dismissed as resistance, the evidence loses value. The mayor says the square will receive temporary furniture, not a temporary guarantee that everyone will agree. At least the benches should make the disagreement more comfortable.

sections.transcript:
Manager: New library cards will be introduced in November. Existing memberships will be transferred automatically.
Reader: Will people lose their borrowing history?
Manager: No. That information will be kept unless a reader asks for it to be removed. Personal details won't be displayed on the public catalogue.
Reader: Some older members may struggle with the online form.
Manager: Paper forms will be provided at the desk, and staff will help during two drop-in sessions each week.
Reader: Good. A digital improvement shouldn't make familiar services harder to reach.
Manager: Exactly. The old cards won't be switched off until the help sessions have run for a month.
Reader: How will members hear about that?
Manager: Notices will be posted in the building and sent with loan reminders. We will also explain the change at the desk. A new card should open access, not become a tiny plastic test of computer confidence.

sections.text: The housing office plans to replace the noticeboards in six apartment buildings. When will the new boards be installed? The published schedule says the work will begin on Monday, but gives no order for individual buildings. Residents also want to know how old notices will be handled. Important information must be copied before the boards are removed. Private phone numbers should not be displayed without permission, and commercial advertisements cannot be added by anyone who happens to find an empty corner. The office initially focused on colour and size. Those choices matter, but they do not answer questions about responsibility. A board can be designed beautifully and still be managed badly. The revised plan names a contact person for each building and explains how notices can be submitted. It also leaves space for handwritten community messages. Clear rules should protect useful communication without turning a request for a borrowed ladder into a formal research application.

sections.text: The swimming pool will be reopened only after the final inspection. New filters have already been fitted, and damaged tiles were being replaced when the residents' committee visited on Tuesday. The changing rooms were not being used during that work. Had the emergency signs been checked before the visit? The manager showed a signed record confirming that they had. However, the accessible entrance had not been tested by users with mobility needs. The committee recommended a practical visit rather than relying only on measurements. Small difficulties can be missed on a drawing. The manager agreed that the route could be assessed by a local access group before opening. The report therefore records substantial progress without calling the pool ready. Some residents want a firm date, which is understandable after a long closure. Still, a date should follow completed checks rather than pressure staff to describe unfinished work as complete. A reopened door is useful only when people can actually get through it.

sections.title: Week 21 · An Exhibition Not Quite Ready
sections.text: The town's photography exhibition will be opened on Friday, but one section may remain closed. The display boards have been delivered, and the captions are being checked by the photographers. The organiser says the lighting should have been tested yesterday. It was not: the electrician was called to an urgent job elsewhere. Visitors are expected to follow a marked route while the final section is prepared. A newspaper described the show as 'fully approved', although only the route through the completed rooms has been inspected. The organiser has asked for that sentence to be corrected. She will have the remaining lights checked on Thursday and will publish an updated access note. Being close to completion is not the same as being ready in every respect. The event can open in a limited form without pretending that every planned feature is available.

sections.text: After the residents' meeting, two summaries appeared in our group chat. One said the caretaker was against the new garden. The other said he supported it. I had taken notes, so I checked his actual words. He said he liked the idea but did not have time to water the beds every evening. He told the committee he could help with repairs at weekends. His objection concerned responsibility, not the garden itself. Both summaries had removed the condition that made his position understandable. I posted a fuller account and asked the writers to correct their messages. Neither had intended to mislead anyone; each had remembered the part that matched an existing opinion. Reporting speech is therefore more than changing pronouns and verbs. It requires selecting fairly. Our final minutes recorded support for the garden and a request for a separate watering team. A useful summary should shorten a discussion without shrinking the people in it into convenient labels.

sections.text: On Monday, the organiser told our student reporter, 'We are preparing a free skills fair. We have contacted local employers, and we will publish the programme on Friday.' The reporter's draft said the organiser was preparing the fair, had contacted employers and would publish the programme on Friday. Those changes preserved the timing of the interview. However, the draft also said every employer would offer a job. That promise had never been made. The organiser had said employers could explain training routes, not guarantee employment. We corrected the article before publication and kept a short quotation beside the summary. The exercise showed that accurate grammar does not automatically produce accurate journalism. A sentence can have perfect backshift and still report an invented commitment. Our editor now asks two questions: does the language match the original time, and does the claim match what was actually said? Both checks matter more than making the event sound impressive.

Supervisor: What did the engineer tell you yesterday?
Assistant: She said she was checking the damaged pump. She said she had ordered a replacement part and could return on Thursday.
Supervisor: Did she promise the system would work that day?
Assistant: No. She said she would test it after fitting the part, but she couldn't guarantee the result before that test.
Supervisor: Good. Our notice must not turn an expected visit into a confirmed reopening.
Assistant: I wrote that the engineer had ordered the part and would return for further work. Is that clear enough?
Supervisor: Add that testing is still required. Residents need to understand the remaining condition.
Assistant: Understood. The original update was careful, but it would be easy to make it sound more certain while shortening it.
Supervisor: Exactly. A summary should remove extra words, not remove the uncertainty that keeps the message honest.

They also asked how long the walk from the college took. The survey leader told volunteers to record answers exactly and avoid suggesting the 'right' response. The final results were mixed: many wanted shelter, while fewer wanted the stop moved. If our report simply said people disliked the stop, it would hide that distinction. The council asked us to explain how the questions had been worded. That was a useful reminder that numbers depend partly on the questions behind them. A survey can sound official while still being poorly designed. Our strongest request became a shelter, supported by specific answers rather than a large but vague pile of dissatisfaction.

sections.text: At our repair club meeting, the coordinator asked members to describe problems honestly. She told us not to promise repairs before checking the items. One volunteer offered to assess electrical equipment, while another refused to handle appliances without the required training. The refusal was sensible, not unhelpful. A third member admitted losing a customer's label and promised to contact the owner. Nobody denied that the mistake had caused confusion. We suggested using numbered trays so each item stayed with its paperwork. The minutes recorded these actions rather than a vague statement that everyone had discussed quality. That distinction matters after a meeting: people need to know who offered, who agreed and who still needs support. A cheerful atmosphere is valuable, but it cannot substitute for clear commitments. The club did not discover a miracle system that evening. It agreed on three small changes that people could actually carry out before the next session.

sections.text: A message claimed that the youth room would close permanently. The actual meeting notes said something different. The manager had explained that repairs would take two weeks and that activities could use the library during that period. A parent had asked whether evening sessions would continue. The manager had promised to check staffing, not guaranteed that every session would run. Someone shortened this into 'They don't know what they're doing', and the temporary move became a permanent closure in later messages. Our youth council published a correction with the confirmed dates and the unresolved question clearly separated. We also asked members not to forward claims without the original notice. The response was mostly positive, although one person complained that the correction was less dramatic than the rumour. That was true. Accurate information often has fewer villains and more conditions. It is still the information people need when arranging transport, work and childcare around a real service.

Reporter: A conditional opportunity is still an opportunity.
questions.explanation: Namunadagi mazmun va manba dalilini kuting; aynan bir xil ibora shart emas. 1–30-dars: bir so‘z, ko‘rsatish yoki o‘zbekcha izoh; hali o‘tilmagan inglizcha gapni talab qilmang. Keyin: qisqa javob + dalil. Xulosa savollarida dalildan ortiq da’vo qilmasin.

sections.transcript:
Reporter: The panel said our project had useful aims but needed a clearer budget. They did not reject the idea completely.
Team leader: What questions did they ask?
Reporter: They asked how we would maintain the equipment and whether volunteers had agreed to the schedule. They told us to separate one-time costs from monthly expenses.
Team leader: Did they offer another review?
Reporter: Yes. They offered to read a revised plan next month. They also suggested testing demand with a small pilot first.
Team leader: Then our next message should explain the work required, not announce either a victory or a disaster.
Reporter: Exactly. I have kept their written comments beside my summary so we can check the meaning.
Team leader: Good. We should be proud of the useful parts and honest about the gaps.
Reporter: A conditional opportunity is still an opportunity. It just arrives with homework rather than a celebratory ribbon.

questions.prompt: Ikki daqiqada yoshlar xonasi xabarini tuzating: tasdiqlangan, va’da qilingan va noma’lum bandlar.
criteria: Uch reported shakli to‘g‘ri.
Savol/va’da kafolat sifatida berilmagan.
Asl manbaga mos betaraf xulosa bor.

questions.prompt: 100–120 so‘zda loyiha guruhiga komissiya javobini yetkazing.
expected: The panel said our project had useful aims but needed a clearer budget. They asked how the equipment would be maintained and whether volunteers had accepted the schedule. They told us to distinguish initial costs from monthly expenses. They also suggested a small pilot to test demand before expansion. Importantly, they offered to review a revised plan next month. This was neither an unconditional approval nor a complete rejection. Our team should use the written comments to prepare specific changes. A fair summary will help everyone understand the opportunity and the work attached to it. We should report both the positive assessment and the conditions instead of choosing the more dramatic version.
criteria: 100–120 so‘z yozilgan.
Kamida uch xil reporting qolipi bor.
Ijobiy baho va talablar ikkalasi aniq.

questions.prompt: Faqat mos fe’lni yozing: The guide ___ us that the cave was closed. (said / told)
questions.explanation: Tell fe’lidan keyin kimga aytilgani bevosita keladi: told us. Say bilan esa said to us bo‘lardi.

questions.prompt: Faqat mos fe’lni yozing: The mechanic ___ that the engine needed oil. (said / told)
questions.explanation: Bu gapda tinglovchi to‘ldiruvchi sifatida berilmagan. Shuning uchun said that ishlatiladi; told odatda kimga aytilganini talab qiladi.

questions.prompt: Faqat bo‘shliqni to‘ldiring: Say/tell, Past Simple: The receptionist ___ me that breakfast ended at nine.
questions.explanation: Tell dan keyin kimga aytilgani to‘ldiruvchi bo‘lib keladi.

questions.prompt: Ko‘rsatilgan xatoni tuzatib, butun gapni yozing: Say qolipi: The guard said us that the gate was locked. Said ni saqlang.
expected: The guard said to us that the gate was locked.
questions.explanation: Say bilan shaxsdan oldin to kerak.

questions.prompt: Told o‘rniga said to ishlating: Nargiza told me that she was leaving.
expected: Nargiza said to me that she was leaving.
questions.explanation: Told me va said to me bir xabarni yetkazadi.

questions.prompt: Faqat A yoki B ni yozing. To‘g‘ri gap: A) He said that he was ready. B) He told that he was ready.
questions.explanation: Tell bu qolipda shaxs to‘ldiruvchisini talab qiladi.

questions.prompt: Zamonni bir pog‘ona ortga surib, faqat bo‘shliqni to‘ldiring: Nina said, ‘I am excited.’ → Nina said that she ___ excited.
questions.explanation: O‘tgan zamondagi said bilan am shakli was ga o‘zgaradi; Nina haqida she ishlatiladi.

questions.prompt: Tasdiq xabarni backshift bilan to‘ldiring, faqat fe’lni yozing: The boys said, ‘We need a ladder.’ → The boys said that they ___ a ladder.
questions.explanation: Need hozirgi oddiy zamondan needed o‘tgan oddiy zamoniga o‘tadi. We olmoshi esa they bo‘ladi.

questions.prompt: Faqat bo‘shliqni to‘ldiring: Backshift: “I like this design,” she said. → She said that she ___ that design.
questions.explanation: Like o‘tgan xabarda liked ga o‘tadi.

questions.prompt: Ko‘rsatilgan xatoni tuzatib, butun gapni yozing: Backshift va egani moslang: Sam said, “I am confident.” → Sam said that he were confident.
expected: Sam said that he was confident.
questions.explanation: He bilan was ishlatiladi.

questions.prompt: Backshift qiling; The twins said that bilan boshlang: “We are hungry,” the twins said.
expected: The twins said that they were hungry.
questions.explanation: We → they, are → were.

questions.prompt: Faqat A yoki B ni yozing. “Rano said that she needed help” gapida yordam kimga kerak? A) Rano bilan gaplashgan kishiga. B) Ranoning o‘ziga.
questions.explanation: She xabar egasi Ranoga ishora qiladi.

questions.prompt: Backshift qiling. Faqat bo‘shliqni yozing, qisqartma ishlatmang: Eva said, ‘I do not eat meat.’ → Eva said that she ___ meat.
questions.explanation: Do not eat bir pog‘ona ortga surilganda did not eat bo‘ladi. Did dan keyin eat asosiy shaklda qoladi.

questions.prompt: Faqat bo‘shliqni to‘ldiring, zamonni ortga suring va qisqartma ishlatmang: The twins said, ‘We are not angry.’ → The twins said that they ___ angry.
questions.explanation: Are not o‘tgan zamonda were not bo‘ladi. Ko‘plikdagi they egasiga were mos keladi.

questions.prompt: Faqat bo‘shliqni to‘ldiring: Backshift: “I cannot find my glasses,” Dad said. → Dad said that he ___ find his glasses.
questions.explanation: Cannot backshift bilan could not bo‘ladi.

questions.prompt: Ko‘rsatilgan xatoni tuzatib, butun gapni yozing: Backshift: “I don't own a car,” he said. → He said that he didn't owned a car.
expected: He said that he didn't own a car.
He said that he did not own a car.
questions.explanation: Didn’t dan keyin asosiy own shakli kerak.

questions.prompt: Backshift qiling; They said that bilan boshlang: “We are not waiting,” they said.
expected: They said that they were not waiting.
They said that they weren't waiting.
questions.explanation: Are not waiting → were not waiting.

questions.prompt: Faqat A yoki B ni yozing. “She said she hadn't received the letter” ma’nosi: A) Xatni olmaganini aytdi. B) Xatni olganini aytdi.
questions.explanation: Not inkor ma’nosini o‘zlashtirma gapda saqlaydi.

questions.prompt: Present Continuous ni Past Continuous ga o‘tkazing; faqat bo‘shliqni yozing: Omar said, ‘I am measuring the wall.’ → Omar said that he ___ the wall.
questions.explanation: Davomiy zamonning backshift shakli was/were + -ing: am measuring → was measuring.

questions.prompt: Present Simple ni Past Simple ga o‘tkazing; faqat fe’lni yozing: Lila said, ‘My uncle owns a bakery.’ → Lila said that her uncle ___ a bakery.
questions.explanation: Owns hozirgi zamondan owned o‘tgan zamoniga o‘zgaradi. Egalik ma’nosi saqlanadi.

questions.prompt: Faqat bo‘shliqni to‘ldiring: Present Continuous ni ortga suring: “I am feeding the birds,” she said. → She said that she ___ the birds.
questions.explanation: Am feeding → was feeding.

questions.prompt: Ko‘rsatilgan xatoni tuzatib, butun gapni yozing: Backshift talab qilinadi: “We live nearby,” they said. → They said that they live nearby.
expected: They said that they lived nearby.
questions.explanation: Present Simple backshift bilan Past Simple ga o‘tadi.

questions.prompt: Backshift qiling; He said that bilan boshlang: “I am learning Korean,” he said.
expected: He said that he was learning Korean.
questions.explanation: Hozirgi davomiy zamon o‘tgan davomiyga o‘tadi.

questions.prompt: Faqat A yoki B ni yozing. “I work nights” gapining backshift shakli: A) She said she had worked nights. B) She said she worked nights.
questions.explanation: Present Simple bir pog‘ona Past Simple ga o‘tadi.

questions.prompt: Past Simple ni Past Perfect ga suring; faqat bo‘shliqni yozing: Ben said, ‘I broke the handle.’ → Ben said that he ___ the handle.
questions.explanation: Broke ning Past Perfect shakli had broken: had + break fe’lining uchinchi shakli.

questions.prompt: Present Perfect ni Past Perfect ga suring; faqat bo‘shliqni yozing: Ada said, ‘I have checked the figures.’ → Ada said that she ___ the figures.
questions.explanation: Have checked backshift qilinganda had checked bo‘ladi; sifatdosh checked o‘zgarmaydi.

questions.prompt: Faqat bo‘shliqni to‘ldiring: Past Simple ni ortga suring: “I left the keys at home,” he said. → He said that he ___ the keys at home.
questions.explanation: Left → had left backshiftidir.

questions.prompt: Ko‘rsatilgan xatoni tuzatib, butun gapni yozing: Perfect backshift: “We have eaten,” they said. → They said that they had ate.
expected: They said that they had eaten.
questions.explanation: Had dan keyin V3 eaten kerak.

questions.prompt: Backshift qiling; Malika said that bilan boshlang: “I have lost my receipt,” Malika said.
expected: Malika said that she had lost her receipt.
questions.explanation: Have lost → had lost; my → her.

questions.prompt: Faqat A yoki B ni yozing. “He said he had broken the cup” gapida qaysi ish oldin? A) Piyolani sindirish. B) Bu haqda aytish.
questions.explanation: Past Perfect xabar berishdan oldingi ishni bildiradi.

questions.prompt: Modal fe’lni ortga suring; faqat bo‘shliqni yozing: Dan said, ‘I will reserve a table.’ → Dan said that he ___ reserve a table.
questions.explanation: O‘zlashtirma gapda will ning backshift shakli would. Undan keyin reserve asosiy shaklda keladi.

questions.prompt: Modal fe’lni ortga suring; faqat bo‘shliqni yozing: Rosa said, ‘I can translate this menu.’ → Rosa said that she ___ translate that menu.
questions.explanation: Can o‘zlashtirma gapda could ga o‘tadi. Bu yerda tarjima qila olish qobiliyati xabar qilinmoqda.

questions.prompt: Faqat bo‘shliqni to‘ldiring: Backshift: “We will wait outside,” they said. → They said that they ___ wait outside.
questions.explanation: Will o‘tgan xabarda would bo‘ladi.

questions.prompt: Ko‘rsatilgan xatoni tuzatib, butun gapni yozing: Modal backshift: “I can juggle,” he said. → He said that he could juggled.
expected: He said that he could juggle.
questions.explanation: Can → could; keyingi fe’l asosiy shaklda qoladi.

questions.prompt: Backshift qiling; She said that bilan boshlang: “I will send the invoice,” she said.
expected: She said that she would send the invoice.
She said that she'd send the invoice.
questions.explanation: Will → would o‘tmish nuqtasidan kelajakni bildiradi.

questions.prompt: Faqat A yoki B ni yozing. “I can lift it” gapining modal backshifti: A) He said he must lift it. B) He said he could lift it.
questions.explanation: Qobiliyat can dan could ga o‘tadi.

questions.prompt: Xabar hozir aytilmoqda. Zamonni ortga surmang; faqat fe’lni yozing: Farida says, ‘I teach biology.’ → Farida says that she ___ biology.
questions.explanation: Says hozirgi zamonda bo‘lgani uchun backshift kerak emas. She egasi bilan teach ga -es qo‘shiladi.

questions.prompt: Hali ham to‘g‘ri bo‘lgan ilmiy faktni backshift qilmasdan to‘ldiring: The lecturer said that the Earth ___ around the Sun. (moves / moved)
questions.explanation: Umumiy ilmiy haqiqatni hozirgi zamonda saqlash mumkin. Topshiriq zamonni ortga surmaslikni so‘rayapti, shuning uchun moves tanlanadi.

questions.prompt: Faqat bo‘shliqni to‘ldiring: Hozirgi xabar, backshift yo‘q: Amir says, “I own two bikes.” → Amir says that he ___ two bikes.
questions.explanation: Says hozirgi zamonda; owns saqlanadi.

questions.prompt: Ko‘rsatilgan xatoni tuzatib, butun gapni yozing: Zamonni ortga surmang: “I am ready,” she says. → She says that she were ready.
expected: She says that she is ready.
questions.explanation: Hozirgi xabarda is ready keladi.

questions.prompt: Hali to‘g‘ri ilmiy faktni backshiftsiz yozing; The teacher said that bilan boshlang: “Ice floats on water.”
expected: The teacher said that ice floats on water.
questions.explanation: Hali dolzarb umumiy haqiqat Present Simple da qolishi mumkin.

questions.prompt: Faqat A yoki B ni yozing. Hali ham to‘g‘ri ma’lumot haqida: A) Backshift qilmaslik mumkin. B) Har doim Past Perfect shart.
questions.explanation: Dolzarblik saqlansa, zamonni saqlash mumkin.

questions.prompt: Faqat egalik olmoshini yozing: Mark said, ‘My passport has expired.’ → Mark said that ___ passport had expired.
questions.explanation: My so‘zi dastlab Markka tegishli. Mark haqida boshqa kishi xabar berganda his bo‘ladi.

questions.prompt: Men ayol kishiman. Tom menga ‘You are the winner,’ dedi. Faqat ega olmoshini yozing: Tom told me that ___ was the winner.
questions.explanation: Tomning you olmoshi gapni hozir yetkazayotgan menga tegishli, shuning uchun I ishlatiladi.

questions.prompt: Faqat bo‘shliqni to‘ldiring: Qizlar gapirdi: “Our bags are heavy,” the girls said. → The girls said that ___ bags were heavy.
questions.explanation: Our xabar qiluvchilar nuqtasidan their ga o‘tadi.

questions.prompt: Ko‘rsatilgan xatoni tuzatib, butun gapni yozing: Erkakning o‘z telefoni: Jasur said, “My phone is broken.” → Jasur said that my phone was broken.
expected: Jasur said that his phone was broken.
questions.explanation: My Jasurning telefoni bo‘lgani uchun his bo‘ladi.

questions.prompt: Ali menga “I will help you,” dedi. Ali told me that bilan boshlang, backshift qiling.
expected: Ali told me that he would help me.
Ali told me that he'd help me.
questions.explanation: I → he, you → me; olmoshlar ishtirokchilarga qarab o‘zgaradi.

questions.prompt: Faqat A yoki B ni yozing. “We are ready,” the players said. O‘zlashtirma gapda we o‘rniga: A) I. B) They.
questions.explanation: Players uchinchi shaxs ko‘plik bo‘lib they ga o‘tadi.

questions.prompt: Dushanba kuni Leo ‘I will return tomorrow,’ dedi. Buni payshanba kuni yetkazyapsiz. Tomorrow o‘rniga the bilan boshlanuvchi iborani yozing: Leo said he would return ___.
questions.explanation: Boshqa kuni xabar berilganda tomorrow asl gap aytilgan kundan keyingi kunni bildiradi: the next day yoki the following day.

questions.prompt: Mira muzeyda ‘I work here,’ dedi. Endi boshqa binodasiz. Here o‘rniga mos bitta so‘zni yozing: Mira said she worked ___.
questions.explanation: Xabar boshqa joydan berilayotgani uchun here o‘rniga there keladi; muzey nazarda tutilmoqda.

questions.prompt: Faqat bo‘shliqni to‘ldiring: Bir hafta keyin yetkazyapsiz: “I saw her yesterday,” he said. → He said he had seen her ___. The bilan boshlang.
questions.explanation: Yesterday boshqa kun nuqtasidan the day before bo‘ladi.

questions.prompt: Ko‘rsatilgan xatoni tuzatib, butun gapni yozing: Boshqa haftada xabar bering: “I'll call next week,” she said. → She said she would call next week. Next week ni the bilan boshlanuvchi iboraga almashtiring.
expected: She said she would call the following week.
She said she would call the next week.
She said she'd call the following week.
She said she'd call the next week.
questions.explanation: Vaqt nuqtasi o‘zgargani uchun the following week kerak.

questions.prompt: Boshqa kun va joyda yetkazing: “I am here today,” he said. He said that bilan boshlang; here → there, today → that day.
expected: He said that he was there that day.
questions.explanation: Joy va vaqt so‘zlari yangi kontekstga moslashadi.

questions.prompt: Faqat A yoki B ni yozing. Bir kunda shu joyning o‘zida xabar berilsa, today va here: A) Kontekstga mos bo‘lsa saqlanishi mumkin. B) Har doim almashtirilishi shart.
questions.explanation: Vaqt va joy o‘zgarishi kontekstga bog‘liq.

questions.prompt: Faqat bog‘lovchini yozing: ‘Have you paid the fee?’ → The clerk asked me ___ I had paid the fee. (if / that)
questions.explanation: Ha/yo‘q savoli o‘zlashtirilganda if yoki whether bilan kiritiladi. Berilgan variantlardan if to‘g‘ri.

questions.prompt: Faqat A yoki B ni yozing. ‘Is the lift working?’ savolining to‘g‘ri o‘zlashtirma shakli qaysi? A) She asked whether was the lift working. B) She asked whether the lift was working.
questions.explanation: O‘zlashtirma savolda ega yordamchi fe’ldan oldin keladi: the lift was working. Savoldagi inversiya saqlanmaydi.

questions.prompt: Faqat bo‘shliqni to‘ldiring: Ha/yo‘q savolini yetkazing: “Are you alone?” → He asked me ___ I was alone. If/whether dan foydalaning.
questions.explanation: Yes/no o‘zlashtirma savol if yoki whether bilan ulanadi.

questions.prompt: Ko‘rsatilgan xatoni tuzatib, butun gapni yozing: So‘z tartibi: She asked whether could I hear her.
expected: She asked whether I could hear her.
questions.explanation: O‘zlashtirma savolda ega yordamchidan oldin keladi.

questions.prompt: If bilan yetkazing; The clerk asked me bilan boshlang, backshift qiling: “Do you need a receipt?”
expected: The clerk asked me if I needed a receipt.
questions.explanation: Do tushadi, need → needed; tartib oddiy gapniki.

questions.prompt: Faqat A yoki B ni yozing. To‘g‘ri o‘zlashtirma savol: A) He asked that I was free. B) He asked if I was free.
questions.explanation: Ha/yo‘q savoliga that emas, if/whether kerak.

questions.prompt: Faqat A yoki B ni yozing. ‘Why did the alarm ring?’ → A) He asked why the alarm had rung. B) He asked why had the alarm rung.
questions.explanation: Wh-so‘z saqlanadi, lekin keyin oddiy gap tartibi ishlatiladi: the alarm had rung. Past Simple backshift bilan Past Perfect bo‘ladi.

questions.prompt: Faqat noto‘g‘ri so‘z tartibini tuzatib, butun gapni yozing: She asked how much did the coat cost. Past Simple ni saqlang.
expected: She asked how much the coat cost.
questions.explanation: O‘zlashtirma wh-savolda did yordamchisi bilan savol tartibi ishlatilmaydi. Cost fe’lining Past Simple shakli ham cost.

questions.prompt: Faqat bo‘shliqni to‘ldiring: Backshift: “Where do you keep the spare key?” → She asked where I ___ the spare key.
questions.explanation: Keep → kept; do tushadi.

questions.prompt: Ko‘rsatilgan xatoni tuzatib, butun gapni yozing: Tartibni tuzating, zamonni saqlang: He asked when would the train leave.
expected: He asked when the train would leave.
questions.explanation: Wh-so‘zdan keyin ega + fe’l tartibi ishlatiladi.

questions.prompt: Backshift qiling; She asked me bilan boshlang: “Why are you laughing?”
expected: She asked me why I was laughing.
questions.explanation: Why saqlanadi, are you → I was.

questions.prompt: Faqat A yoki B ni yozing. “He asked who had called” gapida if kerakmi? A) Yo‘q, who saqlanadi. B) Ha, who o‘rniga if shart.
questions.explanation: Wh-savol o‘z savol so‘zini saqlaydi.

questions.prompt: Buyruqni to‘ldiring; faqat bo‘shliqni yozing: ‘Fasten your seat belt,’ the pilot told me. → The pilot told me ___ my seat belt.
questions.explanation: Buyruq told + shaxs + to-infinitive orqali yetkaziladi: told me to fasten.

questions.prompt: Buyruqni to‘ldiring; faqat bo‘shliqni yozing: ‘Put on your helmets,’ the instructor told us. → The instructor told us ___ our helmets.
questions.explanation: Told us dan keyin to put on keladi. Put on birikmasining ikkala qismi ham saqlanadi.

questions.prompt: Faqat bo‘shliqni to‘ldiring: Buyruq: “Check the lock,” she told me. → She told me ___ the lock.
questions.explanation: Told + shaxs + to-infinitive buyruqni yetkazadi.

questions.prompt: Ko‘rsatilgan xatoni tuzatib, butun gapni yozing: Buyruq qolipi: The coach told us stretch before running.
expected: The coach told us to stretch before running.
questions.explanation: Told us dan keyin to stretch kerak.

questions.prompt: Buyruqni yetkazing; The teacher told the class bilan boshlang: “Open your notebooks.”
expected: The teacher told the class to open their notebooks.
questions.explanation: Your → their, buyruq → to open.

questions.prompt: Faqat A yoki B ni yozing. “He told me to wait by the gate” ma’nosi: A) U darvoza yonida kutayotganini aytdi. B) Menga darvoza yonida kutishni aytdi.
questions.explanation: Object + to-infinitive boshqaga berilgan ko‘rsatmadir.

questions.prompt: Inkor buyruqni yetkazing; faqat bo‘shliqni yozing: ‘Do not feed the deer,’ the ranger told us. → The ranger told us ___ the deer.
questions.explanation: Inkor buyruqda not to + asosiy fe’l qo‘llanadi: not to feed.

questions.prompt: Inkor buyruqni yetkazing; faqat bo‘shliqni yozing: ‘Do not share the password,’ the manager told Kim. → The manager told Kim ___ the password.
questions.explanation: Told Kim dan keyin taqiq not to share shaklida beriladi; do not bu tuzilmada ishlatilmaydi.

questions.prompt: Faqat bo‘shliqni to‘ldiring: Inkor buyruq: “Don't lean out,” she told the child. → She told the child ___ out.
questions.explanation: Inkor buyruq not to + fe’l bilan beriladi.

questions.prompt: Ko‘rsatilgan xatoni tuzatib, butun gapni yozing: Inkor tartibi: The guide told us to not to cross the rope.
expected: The guide told us not to cross the rope.
questions.explanation: Standart qolip told us not to cross.

questions.prompt: Buyruqni yetkazing; The librarian told me bilan boshlang: “Don't write in the book.”
expected: The librarian told me not to write in the book.
questions.explanation: Don’t write → not to write.

questions.prompt: Faqat A yoki B ni yozing. “She told him not to switch it off” ma’nosi: A) Uni o‘chirmaslikni aytdi. B) Uni yoqmaslikni aytdi.
questions.explanation: Not switch off o‘chirishni inkor qiladi.

questions.prompt: Iltimosni ask bilan yetkazing; faqat bo‘shliqni yozing: ‘Please carry this tray,’ the waiter said to me. → The waiter asked me ___ that tray.
questions.explanation: Iltimos asked + shaxs + to-infinitive bilan yetkaziladi: asked me to carry.

questions.prompt: Faqat xato fe’l shaklini tuzatib, butun gapni yozing: The visitor asked us showing her the exit.
expected: The visitor asked us to show her the exit.
questions.explanation: Ask someone to do something qolipi kerak. Showing o‘rniga to show ishlatiladi.

questions.prompt: Faqat bo‘shliqni to‘ldiring: Iltimos: “Please send me the link,” Sara said to Ali. → Sara asked Ali ___ her the link.
questions.explanation: Asked + object + to-infinitive iltimosni yetkazadi.

questions.prompt: Ko‘rsatilgan xatoni tuzatib, butun gapni yozing: Iltimos qolipi: He asked me holding the door.
expected: He asked me to hold the door.
questions.explanation: Asked me dan keyin to hold kerak.

questions.prompt: Ask bilan yetkazing; She asked me bilan boshlang: “Please help my sister.”
expected: She asked me to help her sister.
questions.explanation: Please alohida takrorlanmaydi; my → her.

questions.prompt: Faqat A yoki B ni yozing. “The neighbour asked us to turn the music down” ma’nosi: A) Musiqa haqida ma’lumot so‘radi. B) Ovozini pasaytirishni iltimos qildi.
questions.explanation: Ask + shaxs + to-fe’l harakatni iltimos qiladi.

questions.prompt: Faqat qavsdagi fe’lning kerakli shaklini yozing: The courier promised ___ before sunset. (return)
questions.explanation: Promise dan keyin to-infinitive keladi: promised to return — qaytishga va’da berdi.

questions.prompt: Faqat A yoki B ni yozing. Qaysi variantda ikkala fe’l qolipi ham to‘g‘ri? A) She offered lending a torch, but he refused taking it. B) She offered to lend a torch, but he refused to take it.
questions.explanation: Offer va refuse fe’llaridan keyin to-infinitive ishlatiladi: offered to lend va refused to take.

questions.prompt: Faqat bo‘shliqni to‘ldiring: Reporting verb: She refused ___ the agreement. (sign)
questions.explanation: Refuse dan keyin to-infinitive keladi.

questions.prompt: Ko‘rsatilgan xatoni tuzatib, butun gapni yozing: Offer qolipi: He offered carrying my suitcase.
expected: He offered to carry my suitcase.
questions.explanation: Offer + to-infinitive yordam taklifidir.

questions.prompt: Promise bilan yetkazing; He promised bilan boshlang: “I will repay the money.”
expected: He promised to repay the money.
questions.explanation: Promise to repay va’da berishni ifodalaydi.

questions.prompt: Faqat A yoki B ni yozing. “She offered to drive us home” ma’nosi: A) Olib borishni taklif qildi. B) Olib borishdan bosh tortdi.
questions.explanation: Offered taklif, refused esa bosh tortishdir.
